claim: Long repeat sequences (65 bp – ~6.5 kb) are frequently associated with genome rearrangements, including copy number variation (CNV), in many diverse isolates of Candida albicans.
source: Previously, we identified long repeat sequences that are frequently associated with genome rearrangements, including copy number variation (CNV), in many diverse isolates of the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans (Todd et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Todd et al., 2019) that identified these associations.

claim: Novel, high copy number CNVs are rapidly acquired during adaptation to azole antifungal drugs.
source: Here, we describe the rapid acquisition of novel, high copy number CNVs during adaptation to azole antifungal drugs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing CNV acquisition during drug evolution experiments.

claim: Complex CNVs appear to arise via a dicentric chromosome intermediate and breakage-fusion-bridge cycles.
source: Single-cell karyotype analysis indicates that these CNVs appear to arise via a dicentric chromosome intermediate and breakage-fusion-bridge cycles that are repaired using multiple distinct long inverted repeat sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by karyotype analysis data and inference from the observed patterns.

claim: CNVs are repaired using multiple distinct long inverted repeat sequences.
source: Single-cell karyotype analysis indicates that these CNVs appear to arise via a dicentric chromosome intermediate and breakage-fusion-bridge cycles that are repaired using multiple distinct long inverted repeat sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data showing CNV breakpoints at long inverted repeat sequences.

claim: Removal of antifungal drug can lead to dramatic loss of the CNV and reversion to the progenitor genotype and drug susceptibility phenotype.
source: Subsequent removal of the antifungal drug can lead to a dramatic loss of the CNV and reversion to the progenitor genotype and drug susceptibility phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing CNV loss and phenotypic reversion when drug selection is removed.

claim: The evolution of antifungal drug resistance is an urgent threat to human health worldwide, particularly for hospitalized and immune-compromised individuals.
source: The evolution of antifungal drug resistance is an urgent threat to human health worldwide, particularly for hospitalized and immune-compromised individuals (Perea and Patterson, 2002; Pfaller, 2012; Vandeputte et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this as a known problem.

claim: Only three classes of antifungal drugs are currently available.
source: Only three classes of antifungal drugs are currently available and resistance to all three classes occurred for the first time in the emerging fungal pathogen Candida auris (Chen and Sorrell, 2007; Ghannoum and Rice, 1999; Lockhart et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Resistance to all three classes of antifungal drugs occurred for the first time in Candida auris.
source: Only three classes of antifungal drugs are currently available and resistance to all three classes occurred for the first time in the emerging fungal pathogen Candida auris (Chen and Sorrell, 2007; Ghannoum and Rice, 1999; Lockhart et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature documenting multi-drug resistance in C. auris.

claim: Candida albicans causes nearly 500,000 life-threatening infections each year.
source: The most common human fungal pathogen, Candida albicans, causes nearly 500,000 life-threatening infections each year (Brown and Netea, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Disseminated bloodstream infections of C. albicans have a high mortality rate (15–50%) despite available antifungal therapies.
source: Disseminated bloodstream infections of C. albicans have a high mortality rate (15–50%) despite available antifungal therapies (Pfaller et al., 2010; Pfaller et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical outcome studies.

claim: Most antifungal drugs are fungistatic, not fungicidal.
source: The failure of antifungal drug therapy is likely multifactorial and is compounded by the fungistatic, not fungicidal, mechanisms of most antifungal drugs (Bicanic et al., 2009; Roemer and Krysan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about antifungal drug mechanisms.

claim: C. albicans and other fungal pathogens exhibit significant karyotype and genome plasticity.
source: C. albicans and other fungal pathogens exhibit significant karyotype and genome plasticity (Bravo Ruiz et al., 2019; Chibana et al., 2000; Croll and McDonald, 2012; Gerstein et al., 2015; Magee and Magee, 2000; Selmecki et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2007; Sionov et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 1982; Zolan, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting genome plasticity in fungal pathogens.

claim: The genome plasticity observed in C. albicans isolates is somatic (asexual), based upon the absence of evidence for a meiotic cell cycle.
source: The genome plasticity observed in C. albicans isolates is somatic (asexual), based upon the absence of evidence for a meiotic cell cycle (Alby et al., 2009; Forche et al., 2008; Hull and Johnson, 1999; Magee and Magee, 2000; Tzung et al., 2001), and includes whole genome duplication/reduction, aneuploidy, segmental aneuploidy, and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) (Abbey et al., 2014; Ene et al., 2018; Forche et al., 2008; Forche et al., 2019; Ford et al., 2015; Gerstein et al., 2017; Hickman et al., 2013; Hirakawa et al., 2015; Ropars et al., 2018; Rustchenko-Bulgac, 1991; Selmecki et al., 2006; Todd et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing absence of meiosis and documenting various forms of genome plasticity.

claim: CNVs are highly prevalent in human cancers, resulting in tumorigenesis, metastasis, and increased rates of mortality.
source: CNVs are highly prevalent in human cancers, resulting in tumorigenesis, metastasis, and increased rates of mortality (Beroukhim et al., 2010; Heitzer et al., 2016; Hieronymus et al., 2018; Shlien and Malkin, 2009; Zack et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cancer genomics literature.

claim: Many CNVs occur due to non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) between repeat sequences.
source: Many CNVs occur due non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) between repeat sequences (Chow et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2015; Finn and Li, 2013; Haber and Debatisse, 2006; Hastings et al., 2009; Lobachev et al., 2002; Mizuno et al., 2013; Narayanan et al., 2006; Putnam et al., 2014; Ramocki et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting NAHR as a mechanism for CNV formation.

claim: Antifungal drug stress selects for aneuploidy and CNV formation in diverse human fungal pathogens, including C. albicans, C. auris, and Cryptococcus neoformans.
source: Antifungal drug stress selects for aneuploidy and CNV formation in diverse human fungal pathogens, including C. albicans, C. auris, and Cryptococcus neoformans (Gerstein et al., 2015; Hwang et al., 2017; Muñoz et al., 2018; Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2009; Sionov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing drug-induced aneuploidy and CNV formation.

claim: A recurrent CNV that amplifies the entire left arm of Chr5 in an isochromosome (i(5L)) is sufficient to cause resistance to azole antifungal drugs in C. albicans.
source: In C. albicans, a recurrent CNV that amplifies the entire left arm of Chr5 in an isochromosome (i(5L)) is sufficient to cause resistance to azole antifungal drugs (Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work demonstrating this mechanism.

claim: i(5L) resistance is due to copy number amplification of two genes on Chr5L: TAC1 and ERG11.
source: This resistance is due to copy number amplification of two genes on Chr5L: TAC1, a transcriptional activator of the multidrug transporters (Cdr1 and Cdr2), and ERG11, the target of the azole antifungal drugs.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research establishing the role of these genes in azole resistance.

claim: i(5L) is frequently identified in clinical isolates and is the only CNV known to cause azole resistance in different genetic backgrounds.
source: i(5L) is frequently identified in clinical isolates and is the only CNV known to cause azole resistance in different genetic backgrounds (Ford et al., 2015; Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2008; Todd et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting i(5L) in clinical isolates.

claim: All CNV breakpoints and many LOH breakpoints occur at long repeat sequences in C. albicans.
source: All CNV breakpoints and many LOH breakpoints occur at long repeat sequences (Todd et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior comprehensive analysis of breakpoints.

claim: CNV and LOH breakpoints frequently co-occur within the same long repeat sequences.
source: Furthermore, CNV and LOH breakpoints frequently co-occur within the same long repeat sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior analysis of breakpoint locations.

claim: All (14/14) FLC-evolved isolates acquired one or more whole chromosome and/or segmental chromosome aneuploidies.
source: WGS analysis revealed that all (14/14) FLC-evolved isolates acquired one or more whole chromosome and/or segmental chromosome aneuploidies (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Half of the FLC-evolved isolates (7/14) acquired novel CNVs with high copy numbers (up to 13 copies per genome).
source: Half of the isolates (7/14) acquired novel CNVs (referred to herein as 'complex CNVs') that shared several key features: they had high copy numbers (up to 13 copies per genome), occurred entirely within a single chromosome arm (e.g. within Chr1R in AMS4107 and Chr4L in AMS4702), and were not associated with any centromere (CEN) sequence or the C. albicans repetitive element known as the Major Repeat Sequence (MRS, found eight times within the C. albicans genome) (Chibana et al., 1994; Chindamporn et al., 1998; Lephart and Magee, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data showing copy number amplifications.

claim: Complex CNVs occurred entirely within a single chromosome arm.
source: Half of the isolates (7/14) acquired novel CNVs (referred to herein as 'complex CNVs') that shared several key features: they had high copy numbers (up to 13 copies per genome), occurred entirely within a single chromosome arm (e.g. within Chr1R in AMS4107 and Chr4L in AMS4702), and were not associated with any centromere (CEN) sequence or the C. albicans repetitive element known as the Major Repeat Sequence (MRS, found eight times within the C. albicans genome) (Chibana et al., 1994; Chindamporn et al., 1998; Lephart and Magee, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of CNV locations from sequencing data.

claim: Complex CNVs were not associated with any centromere (CEN) sequence or the Major Repeat Sequence (MRS).
source: Half of the isolates (7/14) acquired novel CNVs (referred to herein as 'complex CNVs') that shared several key features: they had high copy numbers (up to 13 copies per genome), occurred entirely within a single chromosome arm (e.g. within Chr1R in AMS4107 and Chr4L in AMS4702), and were not associated with any centromere (CEN) sequence or the C. albicans repetitive element known as the Major Repeat Sequence (MRS, found eight times within the C. albicans genome) (Chibana et al., 1994; Chindamporn et al., 1998; Lephart and Magee, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of CNV breakpoint locations relative to known genomic features.

claim: Complex CNVs amplified chromosome segments that ranged in length from ~164 kb to ~1.02 MB and contained 57–462 ORFs.
source: These complex CNVs amplified chromosome segments that ranged in length from ~164 kb to ~1.02 MB and contained 57–462 ORFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of sequencing data to determine CNV sizes and gene content.

claim: All copy number breakpoints occurred within 2 kb of one of the 1974 long repeat sequences identified previously.
source: All copy number breakpoints occurred within 2 kb of one of the 1974 long repeat sequences identified previously by Todd et al., 2019 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of CNV breakpoint locations to previously identified repeat sequences.

claim: Complex CNVs were comprised of a two-sided, stair-step amplification pattern that involved at least two distinct long inverted repeat sequences.
source: However, unlike previous observations, these complex CNVs were comprised of a two-sided, stair-step amplification pattern that involved at least two distinct long inverted repeat sequences (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by read depth analysis showing distinct copy number levels at different genomic positions.

claim: The highest copy number in complex CNVs was always flanked by lower copy numbers.
source: Accordingly, each long repeat sequence was associated with two distinct copy number changes, generating regions with different degrees of amplification, with the highest copy number always flanked by lower copy numbers (Figure 1B and C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by read depth analysis shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The same symmetric stair-step copy number pattern (2-6-9-6-2 copies) was observed on two different chromosomes (Chr1 and Chr4) in two different genetic backgrounds (AMS4107 and AMS4702).
source: Surprisingly, the same symmetric stair-step copy number pattern (2-6-9-6-2 copies) was observed on two different chromosomes (Chr1 and Chr4) in two different genetic backgrounds (AMS4107 and AMS4702), indicating that the mechanism is neither chromosome-specific nor strain-specific (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data from multiple isolates shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The mechanism driving complex CNV formation is neither chromosome-specific nor strain-specific.
source: Surprisingly, the same symmetric stair-step copy number pattern (2-6-9-6-2 copies) was observed on two different chromosomes (Chr1 and Chr4) in two different genetic backgrounds (AMS4107 and AMS4702), indicating that the mechanism is neither chromosome-specific nor strain-specific (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of the same pattern in different chromosomes and genetic backgrounds.

claim: The highest copy number identified (2-7-13-7-2 copies) occurred in AMS4104 on Chr3R.
source: Of the eight complex CNVs, the highest copy number identified (2-7-13-7-2 copies) occurred in AMS4104 on Chr3R.
evidence: This claim is supported by read depth analysis of AMS4104.

claim: Both odd and even numbers of amplified copies can be detected in complex CNVs.
source: These findings indicate that the mechanism driving the formation of these complex CNVs uses long repeat sequences, that the amplified number of copies is variable, and that both odd and even numbers of amplified copies can be detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of various copy numbers across different isolates.

claim: Recurrent CNV breakpoints on Chr1R occurred at Repeats 57 and 58 in AMS4107 and AMS4105.
source: For example, recurrent CNV breakpoints on Chr1R occurred at Repeats 57 and 58 in AMS4107 and AMS4105, and recurrent breakpoints on Chr3R occurred at Repeats 134 and 136 in AMS4105, AMS4397, and AMS4104 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by breakpoint analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recurrent breakpoints on Chr3R occurred at Repeats 134 and 136 in AMS4105, AMS4397, and AMS4104.
source: For example, recurrent CNV breakpoints on Chr1R occurred at Repeats 57 and 58 in AMS4107 and AMS4105, and recurrent breakpoints on Chr3R occurred at Repeats 134 and 136 in AMS4105, AMS4397, and AMS4104 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by breakpoint analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All three CNVs on Chr4L amplified a common ~118 kb region in AMS4106, AMS4444, and AMS4702.
source: Interestingly, while the CNV breakpoints on Chr4L were not recurrent and instead occurred at different long repeat sequences, all three of the CNVs amplified a common ~118 kb region in AMS4106, AMS4444, and AMS4702 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of CNV boundaries across multiple isolates.

claim: The long inverted repeat sequences associated with complex CNVs were among the longest (median 1513 bp) repeats.
source: The repeat sequences found at these complex CNV breakpoints were among the longest (median 1513 bp) repeats, and had among the highest median shared sequence identity (96.1%) of all long repeat sequences found throughout the genome (median 516 bp, 95.1% median shared sequence identity), which is similar to repeats associated with breakpoints resulting in CNV, LOH and large chromosomal inversions in C. albicans isolates obtained in the presence and absence of antifungal drugs (Todd et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of repeat sequence characteristics.

claim: The repeat sequences at complex CNV breakpoints had among the highest median shared sequence identity (96.1%).
source: The repeat sequences found at these complex CNV breakpoints were among the longest (median 1513 bp) repeats, and had among the highest median shared sequence identity (96.1%) of all long repeat sequences found throughout the genome (median 516 bp, 95.1% median shared sequence identity), which is similar to repeats associated with breakpoints resulting in CNV, LOH and large chromosomal inversions in C. albicans isolates obtained in the presence and absence of antifungal drugs (Todd et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence identity analysis of repeat sequences.

claim: CHEF karyotype analyses identified a dramatic increase in Chr4 size in two isolates (AMS4702 and AMS4444) with Chr4L CNVs relative to their progenitors.
source: Separation of Chrs 4–7 identified a dramatic increase in Chr4 size in two isolates (AMS4702 and AMS4444) with Chr4L CNVs relative to their progenitors and indicates that these CNVs are intra-chromosomal, rather than extra-chromosomal, amplifications (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by CHEF gel data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The complex CNVs are intra-chromosomal, rather than extra-chromosomal, amplifications.
source: Separation of Chrs 4–7 identified a dramatic increase in Chr4 size in two isolates (AMS4702 and AMS4444) with Chr4L CNVs relative to their progenitors and indicates that these CNVs are intra-chromosomal, rather than extra-chromosomal, amplifications (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased chromosome size observed by CHEF.

claim: Complex CNVs tended to occur within chromosomal regions that were homozygous in the progenitor isolates.
source: Surprisingly, these CNVs tended to occur within chromosomal regions that were homozygous in the progenitor isolates, making it impossible to determine which haplotype was amplified in the CNVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele ratio analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: For CNVs from heterozygous progenitor sequences, the amplifications derived from only one haplotype and the allele ratio scaled with copy number.
source: Nonetheless, for the CNVs from heterozygous progenitor sequences, the amplifications derived from only one haplotype and the allele ratio scaled with copy number (e.g. the percent majority allele was ~50–62–71–64–50 for a 2-3-4-3-2 copy CNV in AMS4106).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele ratio analysis of heterozygous regions.

claim: The growth rate and maximum OD600 was similar between all FLC-evolved isolates and their progenitors in rich medium.
source: In rich medium, the growth rate and maximum OD600 was similar between all FLC-evolved isolates and their progenitors (Figure 2A–D, left panels), with several notable increases in lag phase length (growth curve summary statistics provided in Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: In the presence of FLC (1 μg/ml), the growth rate and maximum OD600 were increased for all FLC-evolved isolates relative to their progenitors.
source: In the presence of FLC (1 μg/ml), the growth rate and maximum OD600 were increased for all FLC-evolved isolates relative to their progenitors, and one isolate (AMS4444) grew better in FLC than in rich medium (Figure 2A–D, right panels, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data in the presence of FLC shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: AMS4444 grew better in FLC than in rich medium.
source: In the presence of FLC (1 μg/ml), the growth rate and maximum OD600 were increased for all FLC-evolved isolates relative to their progenitors, and one isolate (AMS4444) grew better in FLC than in rich medium (Figure 2A–D, right panels, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data comparing growth in different conditions.

claim: Complex CNVs provided increased fitness in the presence of drug without a major cost to fitness in the absence of drug.
source: While each progenitor and FLC-evolved isolate had unique growth trajectories, these observations support, in general, that the complex CNVs provided increased fitness in the presence of drug without a major cost to fitness in the absence of drug.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the growth curve data showing similar growth without drug but improved growth with drug.

claim: Four of the seven isolates with complex CNVs had higher SMG levels than their progenitors in FLC.
source: Four of the seven isolates with complex CNVs had higher SMG levels than their progenitors in FLC, and all seven had higher SMG levels in miconazole (Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by supra-MIC growth measurements shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: All seven isolates with complex CNVs had higher SMG levels than their progenitors in miconazole.
source: Four of the seven isolates with complex CNVs had higher SMG levels than their progenitors in FLC, and all seven had higher SMG levels in miconazole (Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by supra-MIC growth measurements shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: AMS4444 and AMS4105 had the highest SMG level in all azoles tested (0.53–0.73).
source: AMS4444 and AMS4105 had the highest SMG level in all azoles tested (0.53–0.73) and exhibited the highest growth rates and maximum OD600 in 1 μg/ml FLC (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMG measurements and growth curve data.

claim: All isolates that acquired a complex CNV had increased fitness (growth rate and MIC50) and increased tolerance (SMG) to one or more azole antifungal drugs.
source: Therefore, all isolates that acquired a complex CNV had increased fitness (growth rate and MIC50) and increased tolerance (SMG) to one or more azole antifungal drugs, and several isolates had increased tolerance to all azoles tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by comprehensive fitness and tolerance measurements across multiple isolates.

claim: MRR1 was amplified by up to 13 copies in the three isolates with a Chr3R CNV.
source: We found that MRR1, the transcriptional regulator of the multidrug efflux pump Mdr1, was amplified by up to 13 copies in the three isolates with a Chr3R CNV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by copy number analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multidrug transporters CDR1 and CDR2 were amplified within the same CNV as MRR1 in two isolates (AMS4105 and AMS4397).
source: Additionally, multidrug transporters CDR1 and CDR2 map to Chr3R near MRR1, and these genes were amplified within the same CNV as MRR1 in two isolates (AMS4105 and AMS4397).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene locations within CNVs.

claim: MRR1 was always amplified at the highest copy number of the CNVs, while CDR1 and CDR2 were amplified to lower copy numbers.
source: MRR1 was always amplified at the highest copy number of the CNVs, while CDR1 and CDR2 were amplified to lower copy numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by copy number analysis of specific genes within CNVs.

claim: The calcineurin-regulated transcription factor CRZ1 was amplified along with MRR1, CDR1, and CDR2 in AMS4105 and AMS4397.
source: The calcineurin-regulated transcription factor CRZ1, involved in maintenance of membrane integrity and antifungal drug tolerance (Onyewu et al., 2004; Sanglard et al., 2003), also maps to Chr3R and was amplified along with MRR1, CDR1, and CDR2 in the same two isolates mentioned above, both of which had increased tolerance and resistance to multiple azole drugs (AMS4105 and AMS4397, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene locations and copy numbers within CNVs.

claim: The cellular component 'nuclear microtubule' was the only GO term significantly enriched for all genes located within the complex CNVs.
source: The cellular component 'nuclear microtubule' was the only GO term significantly enriched for all genes located within the complex CNVs (p<0.008, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of genes within CNVs.

claim: All four single colony isolates (AMS3051, AMS3052, AMS3053, and AMS3054) were monosomic from the Chr3L left telomere to a shared CNV breakpoint at Repeat 124.
source: All four colonies were monosomic from the Chr3L left telomere to a shared CNV breakpoint at a long inverted repeat (Repeat 124 [blue lines], Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by read depth analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The major difference between the four colonies was the maximum number of copies (3–14 copies) of the adjacent ~146 kb region on Chr3L.
source: Strikingly, the major difference between the four colonies was the maximum number of copies (3–14 copies) of the adjacent ~146 kb region on Chr3L.
evidence: This claim is supported by copy number analysis of the four isogenic colonies.

claim: The MIC50 of the miconazole-evolved colonies increased as the maximum copy number of the complex CNV increased.
source: Importantly, the MIC50 of the miconazole-evolved colonies increased as the maximum copy number of this complex CNV increased (Figure 3B), supporting that in an isogenic background the increase in copy number directly correlates with an increase in MIC.
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC measurements correlated with copy number data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In an isogenic background, the increase in copy number directly correlates with an increase in MIC.
source: Importantly, the MIC50 of the miconazole-evolved colonies increased as the maximum copy number of this complex CNV increased (Figure 3B), supporting that in an isogenic background the increase in copy number directly correlates with an increase in MIC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation observed between copy number and MIC in isogenic isolates.

claim: The four evolved isolates had an additional band of increased size (~854 kb to ~2.16 Mb) consistent with the level of amplification in these isolates.
source: In addition, the four evolved isolates had an additional band of increased size (~854 kb to ~2.16 Mb) consistent with the level of amplification in these isolates.
evidence: This claim is supported by CHEF gel analysis of SacII-digested DNA.

claim: The high-molecular-weight band hybridized to two different probes: an ORF found within the most amplified region of the Chr3L CNV (orf19.344) and CEN3.
source: This high-molecular-weight band hybridized to two different probes: an ORF found within the most amplified region of the Chr3L CNV (orf19.344) and CEN3.
evidence: This claim is supported by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The size and content of the SacII-digested region including CEN3 is consistent with a dicentric chromosome linked via the region containing the different-sized complex CNVs.
source: Thus, the size and content of the SacII-digested region including CEN3 is consistent with the idea that the fragment includes a dicentric chromosome that is linked via the region containing the different-sized complex CNVs found among the AMS3050 derivatives (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CHEF and Southern blot data.

claim: One structural variant was detected at Repeat 124 in AMS3051.
source: One structural variant was detected at Repeat 124 (e.g. Figure 4B), and the other structural variant was detected at Repeat 127 (e.g. Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-read sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Another structural variant was detected at Repeat 127 in AMS3051.
source: One structural variant was detected at Repeat 124 (e.g. Figure 4B), and the other structural variant was detected at Repeat 127 (e.g. Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-read sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Each structural variant combined unique (non-repeat) sequences, that were located up to ~100 kb apart in the reference genome, into a single long-read of only 8 kb – 10 kb in length.
source: Each structural variant combined unique (non-repeat) sequences, that were located up to ~100 kb apart in the reference genome, into a single long-read of only 8 kb – 10 kb in length.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of long-read sequences.

claim: Approximately 50 unique long-reads supported these structural variants.
source: Approximately 50 unique long-reads supported these structural variants and each long-read included a single copy of either Repeat 124 or Repeat 127.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting of supporting long-reads.

claim: The individual long-reads switched between the complement and reverse complement orientation (relative to the reference) within the long repeat sequence.
source: The individual long-reads switched between the complement and reverse complement orientation (relative to the reference) within the long repeat sequence (Repeats 124 and 127, Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by alignment analysis of long-reads shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The long-reads represent fold-back inversions that were presumably mediated by NAHR between distant copies of the long repeat sequences.
source: These long-reads represent fold-back inversions that were presumably mediated by NAHR between distant copies of the long repeat sequences.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structure of the long-reads and known mechanisms of recombination.

claim: The complex CNV located on Chr3L occurs via an accordion-like expansion.
source: These observations, together with the intra-chromosomal CNV expansions detected by CHEF (Figure 3E), suggest that the complex CNV located on Chr3L occurs via an accordion-like expansion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the long-read data and CHEF analysis.

claim: Heterogeneous populations of large and small colonies were observed for each of the four miconazole-evolved isolates in the absence of drug.
source: Heterogeneous populations of large and small colonies were observed for each of the four miconazole-evolved isolates (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony morphology analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The small colony phenotype in the absence of miconazole was due to a fitness defect associated with the dicentric chromosome and/or the monosomic portion of Chr3L.
source: WGS and read depth analysis supported that the small colony phenotype in the absence of miconazole was due to a fitness defect associated with the dicentric chromosome and/or the monosomic portion of Chr3L.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between colony size and karyotype.

claim: Both large colonies (AMS3092 and AMS3093) had resolved the dicentric chromosome and regained the disomic portion of Chr3L.
source: In contrast, both large colonies (AMS3092 and AMS3093) had resolved the dicentric chromosome and regained the disomic portion of Chr3L (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In AMS3092, the dicentric chromosome underwent a recombination event that maintained the complex CNV and heterozygosity across CEN3 and Chr3R.
source: In one case (AMS3092), the dicentric chromosome underwent a recombination event that maintained the complex CNV and heterozygosity across CEN3 and Chr3R.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing and allele ratio analysis.

claim: In AMS3093, the dicentric chromosome underwent a recombination event at CEN3 that returned this isolate to a euploid genotype.
source: In the other case (AMS3093), the dicentric chromosome underwent a recombination event at CEN3 that returned this isolate to a euploid genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and homozygosed all of Chr3L (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing and allele ratio analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: The dicentric chromosome was never completely lost, but had recombined to resolve the dicentric.
source: In both examples, the dicentric chromosome was never completely lost, but had recombined to resolve the dicentric.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that resolution occurred via recombination rather than loss.

claim: Under constant antifungal drug selection (20 μg/ml miconazole), the dicentric chromosome appeared to be highly stable by both colony morphology and karyotype analysis.
source: Finally, under constant antifungal drug selection (20 μg/ml miconazole), the dicentric chromosome appeared to be highly stable by both colony morphology and karyotype analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony morphology and karyotype data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Under continued antifungal drug selection the dicentric chromosome is maintained at the population and single-cell level.
source: Thus, under continued antifungal drug selection the dicentric chromosome is maintained at the population and single-cell level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the stability observed under drug selection.

claim: Removal from the selection pressure promotes the loss/resolution of the dicentric chromosome.
source: In contrast, removal from the selection pressure promotes the loss/resolution of the dicentric chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation of dicentric resolution when drug is removed.

claim: Complex CNVs are acquired rapidly during adaptation to azole antifungal drugs and cause an increase in drug resistance and tolerance.
source: Complex CNVs are acquired rapidly during adaptation to azole antifungal drugs and cause an increase in drug resistance and tolerance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental evolution data and fitness measurements throughout the manuscript.

claim: These CNVs are found across the genome and occur in diverse genetic backgrounds.
source: These CNVs are found across the genome, occur in diverse genetic backgrounds, and are all formed between a set of two distinct inverted repeat sequences that flank the amplified region.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation of CNVs on different chromosomes in different progenitor strains.

claim: Complex CNVs are all formed between a set of two distinct inverted repeat sequences that flank the amplified region.
source: These CNVs are found across the genome, occur in diverse genetic backgrounds, and are all formed between a set of two distinct inverted repeat sequences that flank the amplified region.
evidence: This claim is supported by breakpoint analysis showing inverted repeats at all CNV boundaries.

claim: The mechanism of CNV generation and resolution is driven by successive BFB cycles involving a dicentric chromosome that repairs via homologous recombination between the repeat sequences.
source: Evidence here provides support for a mechanism of CNV generation and resolution back to euploidy that is driven by successive BFB cycles involving a dicentric chromosome that repairs via homologous recombination between the repeat sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including karyotype, sequencing, and long-read data.

claim: The cell-to-cell variability observed for clinical isolates during drug susceptibility assays may be due to the heterogeneity in the copy number of CNVs present within individual cells in a population as well as continued BFB cycles.
source: Furthermore, the cell-to-cell variability observed for clinical isolates during drug susceptibility assays may be due to the heterogeneity in the copy number of CNVs present within individual cells in a population as well as continued BFB cycles.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an explanation for clinical observations based on the experimental findings.

claim: Dicentric chromosomes have been identified in FLC-resistant clinical isolates of C. albicans.
source: Dicentric chromosomes have been identified in FLC-resistant clinical isolates of C. albicans (Selmecki et al., 2006), and suggest that BFB cycles may be possible in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work identifying dicentric chromosomes in clinical isolates.

claim: BFB cycles may be possible in vivo.
source: Dicentric chromosomes have been identified in FLC-resistant clinical isolates of C. albicans (Selmecki et al., 2006), and suggest that BFB cycles may be possible in vivo.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the presence of dicentric chromosomes in clinical isolates.

claim: CNVs with breakpoints at long-repeat sequences have been identified after passage of C. albicans through a mouse model of oropharyngeal candidiasis (in the absence of antifungal drugs).
source: Additionally, CNVs with breakpoints at long-repeat sequences have been identified after passage of C. albicans through a mouse model of oropharyngeal candidiasis (in the absence of antifungal drugs) (Todd et al., 2019), and suggest that complex CNVs could occur in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work showing CNVs in an animal model.

claim: Complex CNVs could occur in vivo.
source: Additionally, CNVs with breakpoints at long-repeat sequences have been identified after passage of C. albicans through a mouse model of oropharyngeal candidiasis (in the absence of antifungal drugs) (Todd et al., 2019), and suggest that complex CNVs could occur in vivo.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation of CNVs in an animal model.

claim: There was very little fitness cost associated with maintaining a complex CNV on a monocentric chromosome.
source: Importantly, there was very little fitness cost associated with maintaining a complex CNV on a monocentric chromosome (Figure 2), which underscores that these CNVs are well-tolerated in C. albicans.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Complex CNVs are well-tolerated in C. albicans.
source: Importantly, there was very little fitness cost associated with maintaining a complex CNV on a monocentric chromosome (Figure 2), which underscores that these CNVs are well-tolerated in C. albicans.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of fitness cost observed.

claim: Stair-step amplifications and fold-back inversions generated via BFB cycles are also observed in human cancers and developmental diseases.
source: Stair-step amplifications and fold-back inversions generated via BFB cycles are also observed in human cancers and developmental diseases (Cheng et al., 2016; Hermetz et al., 2014; Marotta et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on human cancers and diseases.

claim: Amplification of oncogenes (EFGR, ERBB2, and MYC) occurs via BFB in up to ~70% of diverse tumor types.
source: For example, amplification of oncogenes (EFGR, ERBB2, and MYC) occurs via BFB in up to ~70% of diverse tumor types (including breast, colorectal, lung, and liver cancers) (Marotta et al., 2017; Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cancer genomics studies.

claim: In human cells, fold-back inversions causing CNVs occur more frequently (13/21 vs. 3/21) at breakpoints of microhomology (2–8 bp) than at regions of longer homology (296–330 bp, 82–95%).
source: While the exact molecular mechanisms of DNA repair during BFB in human cells remain under investigation (Cheng et al., 2016; Maciejowski et al., 2015; Marotta et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2007), fold-back inversions causing CNVs occur more frequently (13/21 vs. 3/21) at breakpoints of microhomology (2–8 bp) than at regions of longer homology (296–330 bp, 82–95%), such as LINE, SINE, and Alu elements that are present in thousands of copies per genome (Hermetz et al., 2014; Rodić and Burns, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of breakpoint sequences in human cells.

claim: The copy number breakpoints identified in C. albicans only occurred at long-repeat sequences (median 1513 bp) that shared high sequence identity (median 96.1%).
source: In comparison, the copy number breakpoints identified in C. albicans only occurred at long-repeat sequences (median 1513 bp) that shared high sequence identity (median 96.1%) that were predominantly present (10/12 repeats) in only two copies per genome and were always located on the same chromosome arm.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breakpoint sequences in C. albicans.

claim: The rate with which CNVs occur (~1.3×10−6 to ~1.5×10−6 per gene per cell division) is several orders of magnitude higher than the rate of SNVs (~0.33×10−9 per site per cell division) in the absence of selection.
source: The rate with which CNVs occur (~1.3×10−6 to ~1.5×10−6 per gene per cell division) is several orders of magnitude higher than the rate of SNVs (~0.33×10−9 per site per cell division) in the absence of selection (Lynch et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to mutation rate studies.

claim: Formation of a dicentric chromosome can generate continuous cycles of genome instability and can increase population heterogeneity.
source: Our single colony analyses support that formation of a dicentric chromosome can generate continuous cycles of genome instability and can increase population heterogeneity, which is likely to contribute to high rates of clonal interference.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of heterogeneous colony sizes and karyotypes.

claim: Complex CNVs were selected due to the presence of genes that, when amplified, provide a fitness benefit in the presence of azole antifungal drugs.
source: We hypothesize that the complex CNVs identified here were selected due to the presence of genes that, when amplified, provide a fitness benefit in the presence of azole antifungal drugs (Selmecki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed fitness benefits and known gene functions.

claim: Copy number amplification of NPR2 results in increased azole resistance similar to acquisition of the CNV.
source: In support of this hypothesis, NPR2 (within the Chr3L CNV) results in increased azole resistance similar to acquisition of the CNV (Mount et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on NPR2.

claim: ERG11 and TAC1 can confer copy number dependent increases in azole resistance.
source: Other genes like ERG11 and TAC1 (both within the i(5L) CNV) can confer copy number dependent increases in azole resistance (Selmecki et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on these genes.

claim: Every cell that acquires a complex CNV has an increased target size for the acquisition of rare, single nucleotide variants.
source: In addition to the direct effect of gene amplification (i.e. more copies of the gene and its products), every cell that acquires a complex CNV also has an increased target size for the acquisition of rare, single nucleotide variants (Cone et al., 2017; Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from known mutation mechanisms and is supported by citations.

claim: CNVs provide a potential for an increased likelihood of beneficial, drug-resistant point mutations during antifungal drug selection.
source: CNVs therefore provide a potential for an increased likelihood of beneficial, drug-resistant point mutations during antifungal drug selection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased target size for mutations in amplified regions.

claim: Recurrent SNVs in MRR1, ERG11, FUR1, and FKS1 are found in drug-resistant isolates of C. albicans and are recurrent in distantly related Candida species as well, including C. glabrata and C. auris.
source: For example, recurrent SNVs in MRR1, ERG11, FUR1, and FKS1 are found in drug-resistant isolates of C. albicans and interestingly, are recurrent in distantly related Candida species as well, including C. glabrata and C. auris (Flowers et al., 2015; Garcia-Effron et al., 2009; Hope et al., 2004; Morschhäuser et al., 2007; Muñoz et al., 2018; Perlin, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting recurrent mutations.

claim: Exposure to azole antifungal drugs can increase the frequency of LOH in C. albicans.
source: LOH is also an important mechanism of acquired antifungal drug resistance, and exposure to azole antifungal drugs can increase the frequency of LOH in C. albicans (Bouchonville et al., 2009; Dunkel et al., 2008; Forche et al., 2011; Niimi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing drug-induced LOH.

claim: New regions of LOH were identified during dicentric chromosome resolution.
source: Here, we obtained direct evidence that LOH can arise via dicentric chromosome formation and telomere-proximal chromosome loss, the same mechanism that yields complex CNVs. For example, new regions of LOH were identified during dicentric chromosome resolution (e.g. AMS4702 in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and AMS3093 in Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele ratio analysis showing LOH in resolved isolates.

claim: LOH can arise via dicentric chromosome formation and telomere-proximal chromosome loss, the same mechanism that yields complex CNVs.
source: Here, we obtained direct evidence that LOH can arise via dicentric chromosome formation and telomere-proximal chromosome loss, the same mechanism that yields complex CNVs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of LOH during dicentric resolution.

claim: Complex CNVs frequently occurred in regions of the genome that were already homozygous in the euploid progenitors.
source: Finally, we found that complex CNVs frequently occurred in regions of the genome that were already homozygous in the euploid progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele ratio analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Homozygous regions may be the result of prior rounds of complex CNV formation and subsequent LOH in some isolates.
source: We propose that such homozygous regions are the result of prior rounds of complex CNV formation and subsequent LOH in some of these isolates.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal to explain the observed homozygous regions.

claim: Antifungal drug tolerance is the ability of a subpopulation of cells within a susceptible isolate to grow slowly at drug concentrations above the MIC50.
source: Antifungal drug tolerance is the ability of a subpopulation of cells within a susceptible isolate to grow slowly at drug concentrations above the MIC50 (Berman and Krysan, 2020; Rosenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is a definition supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Amplification of genes within transient CNVs is one major route to increase cellular fitness and generate the population heterogeneity that underlies antifungal drug tolerance.
source: We propose that amplification of these genes within transient CNVs is one major route to increase cellular fitness and generate the population heterogeneity that underlies antifungal drug tolerance.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the observed gene amplifications and tolerance phenotypes.

claim: Whole chromosome missegregation resulting in aneuploidy is well-documented in C. albicans and other fungal pathogens.
source: Whole chromosome missegregation resulting in aneuploidy is well-documented in C. albicans and other fungal pathogens (Forche et al., 2009; Forche et al., 2019; Gerstein et al., 2015; Janbon et al., 1998; Ngamskulrungroj et al., 2012; Poláková et al., 2009; Reedy et al., 2009; Rustchenko-Bulgac, 1991; Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2009; Sionov et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting aneuploidy in fungi.

claim: Whole chromosome aneuploidy is likely to be induced (as well as selected) by drug exposure.
source: Importantly, whole chromosome aneuploidy is likely to be induced (as well as selected) by drug exposure (Harrison et al., 2014); however, the mechanisms driving chromosome mis-segregation are not well characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents current understanding in the field.

claim: Cse4/CENP-A is depleted from the centromeres of C. albicans cells exposed to FLC (10 μg/ml), and contributes to an increased rate of chromosome mis-segregation.
source: Importantly, Cse4/CENP-A, which is normally enriched at centromeric DNA, is depleted from the centromeres of C. albicans cells exposed to FLC (10 μg/ml), and contributes to an increased rate of chromosome mis-segregation (Brimacombe et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on centromere function during drug exposure.

claim: The presence of azole drugs may increase the likelihood that a dicentric chromosome is maintained and further increase the likelihood of recombination events that result in complex CNV formation.
source: The presence of azole drugs may increase the likelihood that a dicentric chromosome is maintained and further increase the likelihood of recombination events that result in complex CNV formation.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the observed effects of azole drugs on centromere function.
